The selected current shared files and SOURCE_NOTES.md had no matches for the searched IQC/OZF terms; that is not an exhaustive novelty claim.

## Primary sources and checked boundaries

[Scherer (2022), arXiv:2207.01363](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.01363), especially Theorem 11, equations (25), (30)--(35), Appendix A.5 and section 7. The paper constructs discrete-time constraints with a quadratic terminal term for convex subgradients, using causal and anticausal filters. A finite doubly hyperdominant matrix condition certifies the construction. The displayed filter starts at zero. The stability theorem also needs a coupled storage positivity condition. Its proposed losslessness relative to a more general multiplier test is a conjecture, not a theorem. This supplies a candidate certificate parametrization, not the project's objective-gap constant or an unrestricted converse.

[Fazlyab--Ribeiro--Morari--Preciado, arXiv:1705.03615](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.03615), Theorem 3.1 and equations (3.2), (3.5)--(3.9). The framework allows iteration-dependent algorithm matrices and a Lyapunov function containing objective gap and a quadratic state term. Its sufficient matrix conditions include common fixed-point relations, valid quadratic bounds, nonnegative nondecreasing objective weights and PSD storage matrices. The upper guarantee depends on finding those certificates. It does not establish their completeness or the exact minimax profile.

[Carrasco et al., arXiv:1812.02397](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.02397), introduction and Definition II.4. This multiplier-search paper treats discrete-time SISO LTI systems. Its FIR approximation/completeness statements must not be promoted to a theorem for arbitrary-dimensional, nonstationary gradient descent. It is background only, not a direct bridge.

The current max4 candidate in research/max4_two_sided_residual_join.md has recovered ordinary ConPP after allowing aggregate-coordinate cancellations while retaining nonnegative actual interpolation coefficients. The remaining difficulty concerns independent finite residual penalties and cross-block information. A change of vocabulary is not a new route.

At a block join the filter generally has nonzero inherited memory. It cannot be reset to zero to reuse a theorem whose hypothesis was zero initialization. Account for both boundary states and any function-value terms. The algorithm itself remains the original prescribed GD recursion; auxiliary filter states are proof quantities only, never momentum, averaging or adaptive steps. Check the original last-iterate objective normalization, not just an output-norm or stability bound.

The source conjecture is unavailable as a premise. No completeness, time-varying extension, or lossless compression is assumed. # A finite-polytope projection lift of every finite smooth-convex GD run

**MAIN-AUTHORED JOINT UNVERIFIED CANDIDATE.** This is a new direct Codex
derivation under the operator's explicit direct-reasoning authorization.
It is not a fact and has not been submitted to the verifier. The original
exact-profile minimax target remains OPEN. No mathematical program was used.

## 1. Statement and its scope

Normalize L=1, translate a chosen actual minimizer to0, and subtract the
minimum value. Let f be any globally convex differentiable1-smooth function
on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, with f(0)=min f=0. Fix any finite
predetermined word h=(h_0,...,h_(n-1))>=0, initial x_0!=0 and its ACTUAL run
x_(i+1)=x_i-h_i g_i, g_i=grad f(x_i), including the terminal i=n.

For each sufficiently large auxiliary R>0 there is ONE compact finite
polytope D_R in one extra Euclidean coordinate, containing0, such that

    F_R(z)=max_(v in D_R){<z,v>-||v||^2/2}

is globally convex differentiable1-smooth, grad F_R=P_(D_R), and the
ordinary GD run with the SAME word from z_0=(x_0,-R) approximates the
original function values and horizontal iterates. The new coordinate
is allowed to move under the very same GD update; it is NOT fixed.

The entire minimum set is D_R^polar. The point z_star=(0,-R) is an actual
minimizer, and ||z_0-z_star||=||x_0|| EXACTLY. Consequently this construction
has no growing initial-radius cost. Its closest-minimum radius can only
be smaller, and it is positive when the attained terminal value is positive.

An explicit error estimate is given in Section4. In particular, for every
eta>0 and original run with f_n>0, R can be chosen so that the lifted run,
normalized by its OWN closest-minimum radius, has score at least

    2 f_n/||x_0||^2-eta.

Hence the unrestricted worst-case W_n(h) equals the supremum obtained
over finite-dimensional compact-polytope projection-gradient functions
F_D, allowing arbitrary0-containing polytopes, their entire polar minimum
sets and arbitrary initial points. This is equality of SUPREMA, not a claim
of a finite-R exact representation or an explicit schedule-only adversary.

The construction starts from the already specified original adverse run.
It supplies NO uniform all-word lower comparison and NO improving W upper.
It also does not reduce W to bodies with0 in their relative interior or
to outgoing-optimum-tight transcripts about the chosen nearby minimizer.
Section6 makes that distinction quantitative.

## 2. A finite dual interpolant with an explicit compact domain

For i=0,...,n put

    f_i=f(x_i), y_i=x_i-g_i, delta_i=f_i-||g_i||^2/2,
    ell_i(g)=<y_i,g>-delta_i,
    p(g)=max(0,ell_0(g),...,ell_n(g)),
    K=conv{0,g_0,...,g_n}.

We use only the necessity of the original ordered smooth-convex
interpolation inequalities, accepted fact1252b8823bb5a290:

    Q_ij=f_i-f_j+<g_i,x_j-x_i>+||g_i-g_j||^2/2<=0,

including the optimum sample (0,0,0). In particular delta_i>=0, p(0)=0
and p(g)>=0 everywhere. At each g_i,

    ell_j(g_i)-ell_i(g_i)=Q_ij<=0,
    ell_i(g_i)=<x_i,g_i>-f_i-||g_i||^2/2>=0.

Thus p(g_i)=ell_i(g_i). Define the globally finite function

    phi(x)=max_(g in K){<x,g>-||g||^2/2-p(g)}.

The maximizer is unique, because the objective is1-strongly concave on
the compact convex set K. The usual two optimality inequalities give
firm nonexpansiveness of its maximizing gradient, so phi is differentiable
and1-smooth. More explicitly, if g,g' maximize at x,x', convexity of
p+indicator_K gives <x-x',g-g'> >= ||g-g'||^2. Uniqueness and compactness
also give differentiability by the elementary maximum-envelope argument.

For every g in K, the i-th affine anchor gives

    <x_i,g>-||g||^2/2-p(g)
       <= f_i-||g-g_i||^2/2.

Equality holds at g=g_i. Therefore phi(x_i)=f_i and grad phi(x_i)=g_i
at EVERY original query and the actual terminal. In particular its GD run
from x_0 using h is exactly the given finite run. Also phi>=0 and phi(0)=0.

Set

    M=max_(0<=i<=n)||g_i||,
    Z=max(0,p(g_0),...,p(g_n)).

These are finite constants of the given finite run. Convexity of p and
the finite vertex description of K imply0<=p(g)<=Z on K. Every g in K
has norm at most M, so phi is globally M-Lipschitz. No unbounded dual
domain or uncomputed supremum is used to choose Z.

## 3. The body, complete minimum set, and exact extra-coordinate dynamics

For R>0 define

    D_R={(g,u): g in K, p(g)/R<=u<=Z/R}.

This is nonempty, compact and convex, and contains(0,0). It is a finite
polytope: K has a finite polytope description, and the two vertical bounds
are a finite list of linear inequalities because p is a finite affine
maximum. Degenerate K and Z=0 are included; full dimension is not needed.

Completing the square proves

    F_R(z)=||z||^2/2-dist(z,D_R)^2/2,
    grad F_R(z)=P_(D_R)(z).

The projection is unique and firmly nonexpansive by its two normal
inequalities. These facts also prove directly that F_R is convex,
differentiable and1-smooth. Its definition as a maximum of affine functions
proves convexity. Since0 belongs to D_R, its minimum value is0 and

    argmin F_R=D_R^polar
      ={z:<z,v><=0 for EVERY v in D_R}.

For completeness, if <z,v>>0 for some v in D_R, then tv belongs to D_R
for0<=t<=1 and t<z,v>-t^2||v||^2/2>0 for sufficiently small positive t.
This proves the reverse implication in the minimum-set formula. The
polar is a closed convex cone, not generally a singleton.

The chosen z_star=(0,-R) lies in this COMPLETE minimum set since every
u>=p(g)/R>=0. Its distance from z_0=(x_0,-R) is exactly||x_0||.

Write an actual lifted iterate as z_i=(X_i,-R t_i), with t_0=1.
For any t>=1 and fixed g in K, the objective as a function of u is

    <X,g>-R t u-||g||^2/2-u^2/2,

which is strictly decreasing for u>=0. Thus the optimizing coordinate
is exactly u=p(g)/R. If g_R(X,t) is its horizontal maximizer, then

    F_R(X,-Rt)=max_(g in K){<X,g>-||g||^2/2-p(g)
                             -(t-1)p(g)-p(g)^2/(2R^2)},
    grad F_R(X,-Rt)=(g_R(X,t),p(g_R(X,t))/R).

The ordinary unmodified GD updates are therefore

    X_(i+1)=X_i-h_i*g_R(X_i,t_i),
    t_(i+1)=t_i+h_i*p(g_R(X_i,t_i))/R^2.

For S=sum_(i<n)h_i, nonnegativity of all h_i and0<=p<=Z yield

    1<=t_i<=1+SZ/R^2, for EVERY i=0,...,n.

No coordinate is held fixed, no step is rescaled, and the same static
body D_R is used throughout the entire original chronological run.

## 4. Explicit whole-run and terminal error

Define

    Delta_R=(S+1/2)Z^2/R^2,
    A=Z*sqrt(2S+1),
    Pi_i=product_(0<=j<i)(1+h_j), Pi_0=1.

For every visited t_i and every g in K, the extra objective penalty

    d_R(g)=(t_i-1)p(g)+p(g)^2/(2R^2)

lies in[0,Delta_R]. Let g_K(X)=grad phi(X). The1-strong concavity of
the unperturbed maximization, together with optimality of g_R, gives

    (1/2)||g_R-g_K||^2
       <= [<X,g_K>-||g_K||^2/2-p(g_K)]
           -[<X,g_R>-||g_R||^2/2-p(g_R)]
       <= d_R(g_K)-d_R(g_R)<=Delta_R.

Hence ||g_R(X_i,t_i)-grad phi(X_i)||<=A/R. Because grad phi is
1-Lipschitz and grad phi(x_i)=g_i, the horizontal error E_i=||X_i-x_i||
obeys

    E_0=0,
    E_(i+1)<=(1+h_i)E_i+h_i*A/R,
    E_i<=(A/R)(Pi_i-1).

The last estimate follows by induction from Pi_(i+1)=(1+h_i)Pi_i;
zero steps cause no exception. No claim of a word-uniform bound on Pi_i
is made. All step values are finite for each given finite word.

The value penalty is uniformly bounded as well:

    phi(X_i)-Delta_R<=F_R(z_i)<=phi(X_i).

Since phi is M-Lipschitz and phi(x_i)=f_i,

    |F_R(z_i)-f_i|<=M*(A/R)(Pi_i-1)+Delta_R.

In particular, with the EXPLICIT terminal error

    e_R=M Z sqrt(2S+1)(Pi_n-1)/R+(S+1/2)Z^2/R^2,

we have |F_R(z_n)-f_n|<=e_R and e_R->0 as R->infinity. If Z=0, every
penalty and error vanishes exactly; D_R=K x {0}. All these formulas also
cover degenerate K and M=0, although a positive terminal value forces
M>0.

For a fully explicit sufficient choice to make e_R<=varepsilon>0, put

    C=M Z sqrt(2S+1)(Pi_n-1), E=(S+1/2)Z^2,
    R>=max(1,2C/varepsilon,sqrt(2E/varepsilon)).

This is an analytic parameter choice, not a computational replay.

## 5. Normalization and equality of worst-case suprema

Let r=||x_0||>0. If f_n>0, choose R so that e_R<f_n. Then F_R(z_n)>0.
The initial z_0 is not a minimizer: otherwise its projection gradient
would be0 and every future iterate would be z_0 with value0. The OWN
closest-minimum radius

    r_R=dist(z_0,D_R^polar)

is therefore positive. A closest minimizer exists because the minimum
set is nonempty, closed and convex in finite dimension. Since z_star is
one of its members,0<r_R<=r. Thus

    2F_R(z_n)/r_R^2 >= 2(f_n-e_R)/r^2.

For any desired eta>0 take e_R<min(f_n,eta*r^2/2). This proves the
normalized approximation claim. If the original terminal value is0,
the desired nonnegative lower comparison is trivial and needs no ratio
with a zero lifted radius.

Let W_n^poly(h) be the same supremum as W_n(h), restricted to functions
F_D(z)=max_(v in D)(<z,v>-||v||^2/2), where D is ANY0-containing compact
finite polytope in ANY finite Euclidean dimension, and the original
minimum/initial-point choices remain available. Every such F_D is in
the original smooth-convex class and has a minimizer, so

    W_n^poly(h)<=W_n(h).

For every admissible original positive-score run and every eta>0,
the preceding lift gives an admissible polytope run with score at least
that original score minus eta. Taking suprema gives the reverse inequality.
The zero-score case does not affect it. Therefore the candidate theorem is

    W_n^poly(h)=W_n(h) for EVERY n and EVERY finite h>=0.

For L>0 apply the construction to(f-f_star)/L after translation, then
multiply F_D by L. The update h_i/L times its gradient is the same
normalized update, and the ratio2(f_n-f_star)/(L r^2) is unchanged.
This includes the n=0 case, all zero steps, and arbitrary finite huge steps.

## 6. Why this is NOT a star-tight or centered-body reduction

Relative to the origin, a projection-gradient function F_D has
F_D(z)=<z,v>-||v||^2/2 at v=P_D(z), hence its outgoing optimum row about
the origin is tight. But choosing that origin as the minimizer here would
charge the irrelevant large coordinate R in the initial radius.

Relative to the actual nearby minimizer z_star=(0,-R), the outgoing
optimum slack for the lifted query is EXACTLY

    <z_i-z_star,grad F_R(z_i)>-F_R(z_i)-||grad F_R(z_i)||^2/2
       =-<z_star,grad F_R(z_i)>=p(g_R(X_i,t_i)).

This is generally positive. Thus the lift preserves the original type
of positive conjugate height; it does NOT remove it for free. The whole
polar minimum cone is load-bearing. Replacing D_R by a body with0 in
its relative interior, forcing the minimum to be0, or fixing the added
coordinate destroys the proved normalization/trajectory argument.

The new contribution, if confirmed, is a free-coordinate, true-radius
finite-polytope realization of every finite GD transcript in supremum.
The previous direct fixed-slice epigraph-distance construction did not
by itself give this ordinary lifted-GD statement. No novelty claim against
the external literature is made; no literature theorem is needed beyond
the explicitly accepted interpolation inequalities.

This result does not choose a hard run from h. Its constants depend on
the given finite trajectory, and Pi_n can be enormous. It provides no
dimension-uniform or R-uniform complexity assertion. The original exact
Zhang--Jiang minimax comparison remains OPEN.

## 1. Verdict and precise scope

I found no fatal mathematical gap in the stated finite-run approximation or
the resulting equality of suprema. In particular, the claimed perturbation
inequality has the correct sign, the vertical coordinate really follows GD,
the chosen nearby point is a genuine minimizer, and the denominator comparison
uses the lifted function's own minimum set.

The conclusion is the following normalized statement. Fix a finite integer
`n >= 0`, a finite nonnegative word `h`, and an actual run of a globally convex
differentiable 1-smooth function with a chosen minimizer at zero. Each positive
normalized terminal score can be approached from below by scores from functions

    F_D(z) = max_{v in D} { <z,v> - ||v||^2/2 },

where `D` is a finite compact convex polytope containing zero, in one extra
dimension, and the same unmodified GD word is applied. A different `D` and
starting point may be used for each requested accuracy. The maximization class
must permit the whole minimum cone and arbitrary selected minimizers in it.
Consequently the unrestricted and this polytope-restricted worst-case
SUPREMA agree for each fixed word.

This conclusion does not assert finite-parameter exact interpolation by
`F_D`, attainment within the polytope class, uniform approximation over words,
or a method to select a hard original run from the word. It gives no bound
against the Zhang--Jiang profile. The full derivation below is independent of
the source's favorable conclusions.

## 2. Interpolation anchors: signs and exact identities

Use the original samples `i=0,...,n`, including the terminal sample, and the
optimum sample `*` with `(x_*,g_*,f_*)=(0,0,0)`. The only accepted fact used is
the necessity of the ordered interpolation inequalities in local fact
`1252b8823bb5a290`:

    Q_ij = f_i-f_j + <g_i,x_j-x_i> + ||g_i-g_j||^2/2 <= 0.

The local fact file was read, and its exact verification record has
`verdict="correct"`, `write_error=null`, record ID `5480845b8a751e16`.
No other part of that large fact, including its SDP or attainment statements,
is needed here.

For completeness, the required necessity has a direct short proof. For fixed
`i`, the function `k(x)=f(x)-<g_i,x>` is convex and 1-smooth and has a minimum
at `x_i`. The segment-integral smoothness estimate at `x_j`, with step
`-(g_j-g_i)`, gives

    k(x_i) <= k(x_j-(g_j-g_i))
           <= k(x_j) - ||g_j-g_i||^2/2.

Rearranging gives exactly the stated orientation of `Q_ij`.

Put

    delta_i = f_i-||g_i||^2/2,
    ell_i(g) = <x_i-g_i,g> - delta_i,
    p(g) = max(0,ell_0(g),...,ell_n(g)),
    K = conv{0,g_0,...,g_n}.

The two optimum rows have different roles:

    Q_*i <= 0  gives  delta_i >= 0,
    Q_i* <= 0  gives  ell_i(g_i) >= 0.

Thus `p(0)=0`, while direct expansion, with no change of pair orientation,
gives

    ell_j(g_i)-ell_i(g_i)
      = f_i-f_j + <g_i,x_j-x_i> + ||g_i-g_j||^2/2
      = Q_ij <= 0.

It follows that `p(g_i)=ell_i(g_i)` for every sample, including `i=n`.
The nonnegative maximum with zero does not spoil this equality precisely
because the outgoing optimum row gives `ell_i(g_i)>=0`.

For any `g in K`, the active-anchor inequality `p(g)>=ell_i(g)` gives

    <x_i,g> - ||g||^2/2 - p(g)
      <= f_i - ||g-g_i||^2/2.                         (2.1)

At `g=g_i` equality holds. Therefore the finite dual interpolant

    phi(x) = max_{g in K} { <x,g>-||g||^2/2-p(g) }

has value `f_i` and unique maximizer `g_i` at `x_i`. It will follow below that
this maximizer is its gradient. Since `0 in K` and `p(0)=0`, `phi>=0`;
at zero all the maximized expressions are nonpositive, so `phi(0)=0`.

Every element of `K` is a convex combination of its listed generators. With

    M = max_i ||g_i||,
    Z = max(0,p(g_0),...,p(g_n)),

convexity of `p` gives `0<=p(g)<=Z` on `K`, and the triangle inequality gives
`||g||<=M`. This uses finite known values, not a hidden unbounded maximization.
Maximizing the difference of the affine expressions also gives

    |phi(x)-phi(y)| <= M ||x-y||.                    (2.2)

## 3. Smoothness with a compact, possibly degenerate dual domain

Here is an elementary argument that avoids assumptions of differentiability
of `p`, full dimension of `K`, or interior optimality. Write

    A_x(g)=<x,g>-||g||^2/2-p(g),
    a(x)=argmax_{g in K} A_x(g).

Continuity and compactness give existence, and strict concavity gives
uniqueness. Strong concavity on a line segment from the maximizer to any
`b in K`, followed by division by the segment parameter and its limit to zero,
gives

    A_x(a(x))-A_x(b) >= ||a(x)-b||^2/2.              (3.1)

This argument works at a boundary or in a lower dimensional affine hull.
Use (3.1) for `(x,a(y))` and `(y,a(x))`, and add. The result is

    <x-y,a(x)-a(y)> >= ||a(x)-a(y)||^2.              (3.2)

Thus `a` is firmly nonexpansive and in particular 1-Lipschitz. Evaluating
each maximum at the other point's maximizer gives

    0 <= phi(y)-phi(x)-<a(x),y-x>
      <= <a(y)-a(x),y-x> <= ||y-x||^2.

Consequently `phi` is differentiable with `grad phi=a`, and is globally
1-smooth. Its convexity follows directly from the maximum of affine functions
in `x`. Equation (2.1) now proves both exact values and exact gradients at
ALL the original samples. Induction in the ordinary GD recurrence therefore
reproduces the original finite run for `phi`.

The same elementary argument, with `p=0` and any compact convex domain `D`,
proves differentiability and 1-smoothness of `F_D`. Completing the square in
its defining maximum identifies its unique maximizing vector as `P_D(z)`:

    F_D(z)=||z||^2/2-dist(z,D)^2/2,
    grad F_D(z)=P_D(z).

Convexity here comes from the affine maximum, not from an unjustified claim
that a difference of two convex functions is convex.

## 4. Finite polytope, complete minimum set, and nearby minimizer

For every `R>0`, set

    D_R = { (g,u): g in K, p(g)/R <= u <= Z/R }.

The lower and upper bounds are compatible because `p<=Z` on `K`.
The set is nonempty, closed, bounded, convex, and contains `(0,0)`.
For an explicit finite-polytope justification, start from the finite convex
hull `K x [0,Z/R]`, and intersect successively with the finitely many
halfspaces

    R u >= ell_i(g),  i=0,...,n.

The condition `u>=0` is already imposed by the product. Cutting a finite
convex hull by a halfspace leaves a finite convex hull: retain its feasible
generators and add intersections with the cutting hyperplane of segments
joining feasible and infeasible generators. One can see this by pairing the
positive and negative signed contributions to the hyperplane inequality in
a convex combination. Repeating the finite operation proves the claim
without a full-dimensionality hypothesis. When `Z=0`, the result is exactly
`K x {0}` because `p=0` throughout `K`. If `K={0}`, it is simply `{(0,0)}`.

For any compact convex `D` containing zero, the entire minimum set of `F_D`
is the cone

    C_D = { z : <z,v> <= 0 for all v in D }.          (4.1)

This is the zero-threshold polar CONE, not the body polar with threshold one.
Indeed, `F_D>=0`, and membership in this cone makes all the candidate values
nonpositive. Conversely, if `<z,v> > 0` for some `v in D`, then `v!=0` and
`tau v in D` for `0<=tau<=1`. For sufficiently small positive `tau`,

    <z,tau v>-||tau v||^2/2
      = tau <z,v> - tau^2 ||v||^2/2 > 0.

Hence no such `z` can be a minimizer. This proves (4.1) in both directions.

All elements of `D_R` have `u>=0`, so the fixed point

    z_star=(0,-R)

belongs to `C_{D_R}`. For `z_0=(x_0,-R)`, the exact initial distance to this
actual minimizer is `||z_0-z_star||=||x_0||`. A large coordinate has not been
charged to the denominator. The proof does not replace the actual minimum
set by the singleton `{0}`.

## 5. Actual GD dynamics and the moving added coordinate

At a point `(X,-Rt)` with `t>=1`, for fixed `g` the derivative of the objective
with respect to `u>=0` is `-Rt-u<0`. The optimizing `u` is therefore exactly
`p(g)/R`. The maximization becomes

    F_R(X,-Rt)
      = max_{g in K} { A_X(g) - d_{R,t}(g) },
    d_{R,t}(g) = (t-1)p(g) + p(g)^2/(2R^2).

Let its maximizing horizontal coordinate be `b_R(X,t)`. Uniqueness also
follows from uniqueness of the full projection onto `D_R`. Its full gradient
is

    ( b_R(X,t), p(b_R(X,t))/R ).

Starting with `X_0=x_0`, `t_0=1`, the SAME ordinary GD word gives

    X_{i+1}=X_i-h_i b_R(X_i,t_i),
    t_{i+1}=t_i+h_i p(b_R(X_i,t_i))/R^2.              (5.1)

The plus sign in the second equation is required: the vertical position
becomes more negative. If `S=sum_{i<n} h_i`, induction using `h_i>=0` gives

    1 <= t_i <= 1+SZ/R^2,  0<=i<=n.                 (5.2)

This proves at the same time that the region `t>=1` used to eliminate `u`
contains every actual iterate; there is no circular fixed-slice assumption.
The absolute displacement of the added coordinate from its INITIAL value is
at most `SZ/R`, not zero. It vanishes as `R` grows for this fixed run.

No projection step is substituted for GD: projection is the gradient of the
single static function `F_R`, and the algorithm still subtracts `h_i` times
that full gradient. Neither the word nor the body changes during the run.

## 6. Independent whole-run error derivation

On every visited `t_i`, (5.2) and `0<=p<=Z` give the uniform bound

    0 <= d_{R,t_i}(g) <= Delta_R := (S+1/2)Z^2/R^2,
    for every g in K.                               (6.1)

Fix such a visited pair `(X,t)`, put `a=grad phi(X)` and `b=b_R(X,t)`.
Optimality in the PERTURBED maximum gives

    A_X(b)-d(b) >= A_X(a)-d(a).

Combining this with (3.1) yields, with the indicated sign,

    ||a-b||^2/2 <= A_X(a)-A_X(b)
                <= d(a)-d(b) <= Delta_R.            (6.2)

In particular, the source does not need the looser bound `2 Delta_R` on the
right: the nonnegative perturbation lies in `[0,Delta_R]`, whose oscillation
is at most `Delta_R`. With `A=Z sqrt(2S+1)`, (6.2) gives

    ||b_R(X_i,t_i)-grad phi(X_i)|| <= A/R.

Let `E_i=||X_i-x_i||` and `Pi_i=product_{j<i}(1+h_j)`. Using (5.1), the original
GD update, interpolation of `g_i`, and 1-Lipschitz continuity of `grad phi`,

    E_{i+1} <= (1+h_i)E_i + h_i A/R,
    E_0=0.

Induction, including `h_i=0`, gives exactly

    E_i <= (A/R)(Pi_i-1).                           (6.3)

In fact the full iterates, after subtracting the nearby minimizer, satisfy

    ||(z_i-z_star)-(x_i,0)|| <= (A/R)(Pi_i-1)+SZ/R.

Thus the moving extra coordinate also converges to zero in the translated
trajectory; there is no hidden order-one displacement in that direction.

Taking maxima in (6.1) gives

    phi(X_i)-Delta_R <= F_R(z_i) <= phi(X_i).

Use (2.2), (6.3), and `phi(x_i)=f_i` to obtain

    |F_R(z_i)-f_i|
       <= M A(Pi_i-1)/R + Delta_R.

At the actual terminal iterate this is exactly the source's estimate

    e_R = M Z sqrt(2S+1)(Pi_n-1)/R
          + (S+1/2)Z^2/R^2.                        (6.4)

All constants are finite for each fixed finite actual run and each finite
word, however large its entries. Given `epsilon>0`, write

    C=M Z sqrt(2S+1)(Pi_n-1),  E=(S+1/2)Z^2.

Then `R>=max(1,2C/epsilon,sqrt(2E/epsilon))` makes each term of (6.4) at most
`epsilon/2`. This also works when either or both constants vanish. It proves
convergence without invoking an asymptotic interchange of unbounded words.

## 7. Own closest radius and equality of suprema

Set `r=||x_0||>0`. If `f_n>0`, choose `R` with `e_R<f_n`, so `F_R(z_n)>0`.
If `z_0` were a minimizer, its gradient would be zero and every GD step would
leave it fixed, for ANY finite prescribed steps. That would give terminal
value zero, a contradiction. Thus `z_0` is outside the closed cone `C_{D_R}`.

The distance

    r_R=dist(z_0,C_{D_R})

is positive. A closest point exists: zero belongs to the closed set, so a
minimizing sequence can be confined to a bounded ball, and finite-dimensional
compactness gives a minimizing limit. Because `z_star` is another member,

    0 < r_R <= r.

The lower numerator `f_n-e_R` is strictly positive. This sign matters when
comparing denominators, and it gives

    2 F_R(z_n)/r_R^2
      >= 2(f_n-e_R)/r_R^2
      >= 2(f_n-e_R)/r^2.                            (7.1)

Choosing `e_R<min(f_n,eta r^2/2)` makes (7.1) exceed
`2f_n/r^2-eta`. No claim that `r_R` equals or tends to `r` is needed.
Indeed, the normalized scores themselves need not converge to the original
score; the one-sided comparison is the correct assertion. One could already
obtain the required comparison using the selected minimizer `z_star`; the
own-closest comparison is a valid strengthening.

For `f_n=0`, the original score is zero, and the restricted supremum is
nonnegative. No ratio with `r_R=0` is necessary. In the original definition,
a start that is itself a minimizer but differs from the selected minimizer
also has score zero and causes no problem.

For precision, at smoothness one define the restricted supremum over every
finite dimension, every compact convex finite polytope `D` containing zero,
every `z_* in C_D`, and every `z_0!=z_*`. Every such `F_D` is a legal original
instance, so `W_n^poly(h)<=W_n(h)`. Conversely, (7.1) applies to each original
positive-score instance and each `eta>0`; its lifted instance is among the
restricted choices. Taking the two suprema yields

    W_n^poly(h)=W_n(h).

The quantifier order used is

    for every finite n and finite h>=0,
    for every original actual instance and every eta>0,
    there exists a finite R and one admissible D_R.

It is NOT a single choice of `R` for all instances or all words. Equality is
pointwise in `h`; no interchange of `inf_h` and an approximation limit is
used. Taking `inf_h` AFTER this equality gives equality of the corresponding
minimax formulations, but supplies no numerical or asymptotic bound for them.

There is also no hidden infinite-score issue. For any original instance,
Lipschitz continuity of the gradient at a chosen minimizer gives
`||x_i-x_*||<=Pi_i||x_0-x_*||`; smoothness at that minimizer then gives
`2(f_n-f_*)<=||x_n-x_*||^2`. Thus `W_n(h)<=Pi_n^2<infinity` at smoothness one.
The same bound applies to each lifted function with ITS closest minimizer.

## 8. Normalization and boundary cases

For an original `L>0`, chosen minimizer `x_*`, and minimum value `f_*`, apply
the preceding argument to

    tilde f(x)=(f(x_*+x)-f_*)/L.

Its gradient is `grad f(x_*+x)/L`, so its step `h_i` is exactly the original
step `h_i/L` after translation. Restore scale by using `L F_D` in the
original problem: its gradient is `L P_D`, and the update `h_i/L` again
gives the same lifted run. Its score is

    2[L F_D(z_n)]/[L ||z_0-z_*||^2]
      =2F_D(z_n)/||z_0-z_*||^2.

Accordingly, for general `L` the restricted functions are `L F_D`. A bare
`F_D` has gradient `P_D` and belongs to the normalized `L=1` statement.
The draft's final scaling paragraph supplies this qualification; it should
remain explicit in any standalone theorem statement.

The following cases require no additional hypothesis:

- `n=0`: `S=0`, `Pi_0=1`, horizontal error is zero and the value error is at
  most `Z^2/(2R^2)`. The single sampled point is also the terminal point.
- All steps zero: positions and `t_i` stay fixed; repeated sample anchors are
  harmless. The same estimate applies.
- Some zero steps: (5.1) and (6.3) simply leave the corresponding errors
  unchanged; no strict-Slater or distinct-point condition appears.
- Arbitrarily huge but finite steps: `S` and `Pi_n` may be very large, but
  remain finite, and the explicit choice of `R` remains valid.
- `Z=0`: convexity and nonnegativity force `p=0` throughout `K`; the lifted
  body is `K x {0}`, every perturbation is zero, and the run is exact.
- `M=0`: all sample gradients vanish. Each actual sampled point is a
  minimizer, all sample values are zero, and `D_R={0}`. The zero-score clause
  handles the closest-radius degeneracy.
- Lower dimensional `K` or `D_R`: all uniqueness and concavity arguments
  are in the ambient Euclidean norm restricted to a convex set, so no
  affine-span interior assumption is used.

Negative steps and an infinite horizon are outside the declared scope.
The present proof specifically uses nonnegativity to maintain `t_i>=1`.

## 9. Positive slack: analytic structural attacks

For `v=P_D(z)`, the defining maximum gives

    F_D(z)=<z,v>-||v||^2/2.

At any minimizer `a in C_D`, the outgoing optimum slack is therefore

    <z-a,v>-F_D(z)-||v||^2/2 = -<a,v> >= 0.          (9.1)

It is zero at `a=0`, but need not be zero at another minimizer. At the
specific nearby `z_star=(0,-R)`, use the exact second gradient component
from Section 5 to get

    -<z_star,grad F_R(z_i)>=p(b_R(X_i,t_i)).          (9.2)

The positive slack is thus retained exactly as stated. Moreover, `p` is
Lipschitz with constant `B=max_i||x_i-g_i||`, since it is a finite maximum
of affine functions with those slopes and the zero function. From (6.3),

    ||b_R(X_i,t_i)-g_i|| <= A Pi_i/R,
    |p(b_R(X_i,t_i))-p(g_i)| <= B A Pi_i/R.

Whenever the original outgoing optimum slack `p(g_i)` is positive, it stays
positive at this nearby minimizer for all sufficiently large `R`.

Here is a fully analytic attack on the possibility that choosing the OWN
closest minimizer might secretly force slack to zero. Take `n=0`,

    f(x)=x^2/4,  x_0=1,  g_0=1/2,  f_0=1/4.

Then

    K=[0,1/2],
    p(g)=max(0,g/2-1/8),
    Z=1/8.

The body lies in the nonnegative quadrant and contains nonzero horizontal
and vertical axis segments: `(g,0)` for `0<=g<=1/4` and `(0,u)` for
`0<=u<=1/(8R)`. Consequently its full polar cone is exactly the negative
quadrant. For `z_0=(1,-R)`, its unique closest minimizer is `(0,-R)`, at
distance one.

On the active segment `1/4<g<1/2`, the reduced objective derivative is

    1/2-g-(g/2-1/8)/(2R^2).

It is positive at the left endpoint and negative at the right endpoint.
Solving its linear zero gives the actual horizontal projection

    g_R=(8R^2+1)/[4(4R^2+1)],
    p(g_R)=R^2/[2(4R^2+1)] > 0.

Both inequalities `1/4<g_R<1/2` hold for every `R>0`, so this branch check
is exact. Direct substitution, using (2.1) with equality on that segment,
gives

    F_R(1,-R)=1/4-1/[32(4R^2+1)].

Thus the own-closest normalized score tends to `1/2`, while the outgoing
optimum slack at that OWN closest minimizer tends to `1/8`, not to zero.
This example supports the declared distinction; it is not a counterexample
to the reduction. All formulas in this example were derived analytically,
with no arithmetic program or solver.

A second structural test is `f(x)=||x||^2/2` under ANY finite word, including
overshooting words. Here `x_i=g_i`, every `delta_i=0`, every anchor is zero,
and `Z=0`. The resulting body `K x {0}` reproduces the entire finite run
exactly because it contains every `g_i=x_i`. This confirms that the
zero-height degeneration is compatible with large-step trajectories.

Finally, if `0` is in the relative interior of `D`, every vector in its polar
cone is orthogonal to `span(D)`: small positive and negative multiples of
every direction in that span occur in `D`, forcing both polar inequalities.
Equation (9.1) is then zero for EVERY minimizer. The positive-slack example
shows why the present construction cannot simply be declared a reduction to
that restricted representation. It does not disprove some separate equality
of suprema for a different restricted family; it establishes that such a
claim is absent from, and unsupported by, this proof.

## 10. Limitations, editorial qualifications, and resources

No repair is required for the stated theorem at its declared scope. To avoid
future scope inflation, a standalone version should retain these details:

1. Use `L F_D` at general smoothness `L`; reserve `grad F_D=P_D` for the

2. Define the polar by the explicit `<=0` inequalities and allow all its

3. State approximation and equality of suprema, not exact finite-`R`
   representation or attainment in the restricted class.
4. Preserve instance-dependent `R` and the factor `Pi_n`; there is no uniform
   word-independent error constant.
5. Keep positive outgoing-optimum slack about the nearby minimizer. The
   construction depends on the original adverse run and does not select one
   from `h` or establish any target-profile lower bound.

## 1. Exact horizontal lift of one strict-smoothness run

Let f be convex, differentiable and ell-smooth for0<ell<1, with minimum0
attained at0. Fix any finite nonnegative word h of length n and its actual
jets x_i,g_i,f_i, i=0,...,n. Define

    eta_i=<x_i,g_i>-f_i-||g_i||^2/2,
    H_i=sum_(t<i)h_t eta_t,
    Q_ji=f_j-f_i+<g_j,x_i-x_j>+||g_j-g_i||^2/2.

Include a reference label star with g_star=eta_star=f_star=x_star=0.
The standard ell-smooth interpolation inequality gives

    Q_ji <= -gamma||g_j-g_i||^2,
    gamma=(1-ell)/(2ell)>0.

The optimum rows imply eta_i>=gamma||g_i||^2>=0, and
f_i-||g_i||^2/2>=gamma||g_i||^2. If g_i=g_j, both convexity inequalities
give f_i-f_j=<g_i,x_i-x_j>, hence eta_i=eta_j. Thus an equal-gradient pair
has no eta difference even if its original positions differ. If g_i=0,
then f_i=eta_i=0.

For a finite R>0 let

    v_i=(g_i,eta_i/R),
    D_R=conv{0,v_0,...,v_n},
    z_i=(x_i,-R-H_i/R),
    z_star=(0,-R).

This body has AT MOST n+2 vertices and lies in one extra coordinate.
Every eta_i>=0, so z_star belongs to the whole minimum cone D_R^polar of
F_R(z)=max_(v in D_R)(<z,v>-||v||^2/2). Its selected initial distance is
exactly||x_0||.

The exact normal-condition identity for any sampled i and any j including

# Joint candidate: sparse exact lifts and simplex universality for finite GD words

**JOINT UNVERIFIED THEOREM CANDIDATE.** Analytical result of the ONE fresh
bounded allocation in this directory. The sparse main-authored mechanism
survives independent checking, and the proposed simplex extension admits the
explicit proof below. Neither result is a verifier-accepted project fact.
The original exact Zhang--Jiang minimax target remains OPEN.

The complete frozen source was `MAIN_CANDIDATE_UNVERIFIED.md`, 6752 bytes,
actual SHA256
`cd09d624628958d04d5728ca7fd6b0e8fa489ea8c72021d2d3151b8331870963`.
It was read completely and was not edited. The earlier epigraph audit is not
used as mathematical authority; the needed elementary facts are derived here.

## 1. Strongest conclusion established by this analytical argument

Fix an integer `n>=0` and a finite word `h=(h_0,...,h_{n-1})>=0`. Let

    S = sum_{t<n} h_t,
    p = #{t<n : h_t>0}.

Normalize smoothness to one. Let `W_n(h)` be the original unrestricted
worst-case normalized terminal objective. Define `W_n^simplex(h)` by
restricting its functions to

    F_D(q) = max_{v in D} { <q,v>-||v||^2/2 },

where, in some Euclidean dimension `m` with `1<=m<=p+1`,

    D = conv{0,w_1,...,w_m},

and `w_1,...,w_m` are linearly independent. Thus `D` is a genuine
full-dimensional `m`-simplex and zero is one of its vertices. Keep arbitrary
initial points and the complete actual minimum set, with the original choice
of minimizer in the denominator. The candidate conclusion is

    W_n^simplex(h) = W_n(h).                        (1.1)

Equivalently, every positive-score original finite run can be approximated
from below in normalized terminal score by such a simplex function under
the SAME unmodified GD word. The new run can be normalized by its OWN closest
minimizer. There are at most `p+2<=n+2` vertices, in dimension at most
`p+1<=n+1`, independently of the original ambient dimension.

More precisely, for a given strict-smoothness run, `m` can be taken to be its
number of distinct nonzero sampled gradients, including the terminal sample.
The construction gives exactly `m+1` simplex vertices and dimension `m`.
No claim that this dimension bound is universally minimal is made.

For an arbitrary original 1-smooth run, first use `c f` with `c<1` close to
one. For that strict-smoothness run, the pre-compression lift reproduces all
ORIGINAL HORIZONTAL ITERATES exactly and has an explicit value correction.
Compression preserves the lifted values and GD dynamics; it need not retain
the original horizontal coordinates as a distinguished coordinate block.

Equation (1.1) is equality of SUPREMA. It is not finite-parameter exact
representation of an arbitrary 1-smooth run or attainment within the simplex
class. It neither chooses an adverse original run from `h` nor compares the
score with `U_n^ZJ`. At general smoothness `L`, the restricted class is
`L F_D`, with step `h_i/L`.

## 2. Elementary projection facts and the complete minimum set

For a nonempty compact convex set `D`, the maximizer defining `F_D` is unique:
completing the square identifies it with the unique nearest point `P_D(q)`.
For `v in D`, the exact characterization is

    P_D(q)=v  iff  <q-v,w-v><=0 for every w in D.     (2.1)

Necessity follows by differentiating the squared distance on the segment
from `v` to `w` at zero. For sufficiency, expand

    ||q-w||^2 = ||q-v||^2 + ||w-v||^2
                -2<q-v,w-v> >= ||q-v||^2.

For a finite convex hull it is enough to check every generating point,
because the left side of (2.1) is affine in `w`.

The two normal inequalities for `v=P_D(q)` and `v'=P_D(q')` imply

    <q-q',v-v'> >= ||v-v'||^2.

Thus the projection is 1-Lipschitz. Evaluating the affine maxima at each
other's optimizers gives

    0 <= F_D(q')-F_D(q)-<P_D(q),q'-q>
      <= <P_D(q')-P_D(q),q'-q> <= ||q'-q||^2.

Consequently `F_D` is differentiable with gradient `P_D` and is globally
1-smooth. It is convex as a maximum of affine functions of `q` and finite
because `D` is compact.

When `0 in D`, the minimum is zero and its COMPLETE minimum set is the cone

    C_D = { a : <a,v><=0 for every v in D }.          (2.2)

Membership makes every defining expression nonpositive, while `v=0` gives
zero. Conversely, if `<a,v>>0` for some `v in D`, then `theta v in D` for
`0<=theta<=1`, and

    <a,theta v>-||theta v||^2/2 > 0

for sufficiently small positive `theta`. Thus `a` is not a minimizer.
The polar here always means the cone with threshold ZERO, not a body polar
with threshold one. It is nonempty, closed, and convex, so every point has
a closest point in it. Existence follows, for example, by restricting a
distance-minimizing sequence to a bounded ball and taking a convergent
subsequence.

## 3. Strict smoothness supplies the necessary strict rows

Let `0<ell<1`, let `f` be convex differentiable and ell-smooth, and translate
and subtract its chosen optimum so that `f(0)=min f=0`. Use its ACTUAL GD
samples `i=0,...,n`, including the terminal sample, with

    x_{i+1}=x_i-h_i g_i,
    g_i=grad f(x_i),  f_i=f(x_i).

Add a reference label `*` with `x_*=g_*=f_*=0`. Define

    Q_ji = f_j-f_i+<g_j,x_i-x_j>+||g_j-g_i||^2/2,
    gamma = (1-ell)/(2ell)>0.

The ell-smooth interpolation necessity is

    Q_ji <= -gamma ||g_j-g_i||^2.                   (3.1)

This is the smoothness-scaled necessity part of accepted local fact
`1252b8823bb5a290`; none of its duality or attainment conclusions is used.
One can also derive the precise orientation directly: the convex function
`k(x)=f(x)-<g_j,x>` has a minimum at `x_j`, and an ell-smooth descent step
from `x_i` of length `1/ell` gives

    k(x_j) <= k(x_i-(g_i-g_j)/ell)
             <= k(x_i)-||g_i-g_j||^2/(2ell).

Rearrange and add the `||g_i-g_j||^2/2` term to obtain (3.1).

Put

    eta_i = <x_i,g_i>-f_i-||g_i||^2/2,
    H_i = sum_{t<i} h_t eta_t,
    eta_* = 0.

The optimum row `Q_{i,*}=-eta_i` gives

    eta_i >= gamma ||g_i||^2 >= 0,                 (3.2)

and `Q_{*,i}=-f_i+||g_i||^2/2` gives

    f_i-||g_i||^2/2 >= gamma ||g_i||^2.             (3.3)

In particular every nonzero gradient has STRICTLY positive `eta_i`.
If `g_i=0`, convexity makes `x_i` a minimizer, so `f_i=eta_i=0`.
All later gradients and positions then remain zero-gradient/stationary.

If `g_i=g_j=g`, the two elementary convexity inequalities force

    f_i-f_j=<g,x_i-x_j>.

Therefore `eta_i=eta_j`, and direct substitution gives `Q_ji=0`.
The same conclusion applies to equal zero gradients and to the reference
label. Distinct positions with the same gradient need not be identified as
positions; only their gradient/height vertex labels will be identified.

## 4. Mechanism 1: exact sparse normal-guard construction

For `R>0`, define

    v_i=(g_i,eta_i/R),  v_*=0,
    D_R=conv{0,v_0,...,v_n},
    z_i=(x_i,-R-H_i/R),
    a_R=(0,-R).

This is a compact finite polytope in one extra coordinate, with at most
`n+2` generating points. The point `a_R` belongs to its full minimum cone
because `<a_R,v_i>=-eta_i<=0`. For `z_0=(x_0,-R)`,

    ||z_0-a_R||=||x_0||.                           (4.1)

The claimed identity is exact. For every physical sample `i` and every
`j in {*,0,...,n}`,

    <z_i-v_i,v_j-v_i>
      = <x_i-g_i,g_j-g_i>-(eta_j-eta_i)
        -(H_i+eta_i)(eta_j-eta_i)/R^2
      = Q_ji-(H_i+eta_i)(eta_j-eta_i)/R^2.          (4.2)

For clarity, the middle terms expand to

    <x_i-g_i,g_j-g_i>-(eta_j-eta_i)
      = f_j-f_i+<g_j,x_i-x_j>+||g_j-g_i||^2/2.

This checks both the orientation `Q_ji` and the sign of the vertical
correction. No position associated with the reference `*` appears in the
normal test other than through the zero jet in `Q_*i`.

If `g_i=g_j`, both terms in (4.2) vanish. Otherwise `-Q_ji>0` by (3.1).
Define the data-dependent finite number

    A = max_{i=0,...,n; j in {*,0,...,n}; g_i!=g_j}
          (H_i+eta_i)(eta_i-eta_j)_+ / (-Q_ji),      (4.3)

with maximum over an empty set equal to zero. Finiteness follows from
finitely many finite data and strictly positive denominators. Here
`H_i+eta_i>=0` uses the nonnegative steps.

For `R^2>=A`, all expressions in (4.2) are nonpositive. By (2.1),

    P_{D_R}(z_i)=v_i,  for EVERY physical i=0,...,n. (4.4)

The prospective positions satisfy

    z_{i+1}=z_i-h_i v_i,                            (4.5)

because `H_{i+1}=H_i+h_i eta_i`. Equations (4.4)--(4.5), by induction from
the stated initial point, prove that these are the ACTUAL ordinary GD
iterates on the single fixed function `F_{D_R}`. All original horizontal
positions are reproduced exactly. The added coordinate moves by
`-h_i eta_i/R`; it is not held fixed.

The value at every actual sample is also exact:

    F_{D_R}(z_i)
      = <z_i,v_i>-||v_i||^2/2
      = f_i-C_i/R^2,
    C_i = eta_i H_i+eta_i^2/2 >= 0.                (4.6)

The optimum/reference row is included in the guard; it is not left to a
heuristic value estimate. If `g_i!=0`, (4.4) already implies positive value
via `F_{D_R}(z_i)>=||v_i||^2/2>0`. Taking `R` larger also makes the explicit
correction in (4.6) as small as desired.

This completes Mechanism 1 with no gap found. If only `R^2=A` is used, some
distinct-vertex rows may be equalities; that boundary is insufficient for
the generic perturbation proposal. The next section deliberately chooses
strict quantitative slack instead.

## 5. Quantitative strict margins, including zero-gradient samples

Suppose at least one sampled gradient is nonzero. List the distinct nonzero
gradient values as `g^1,...,g^m`, with their well-defined heights
`eta^1,...,eta^m`. Write

    g^0=0,  eta^0=0,
    a(i) in {0,...,m},
    g_i=g^{a(i)},  eta_i=eta^{a(i)}.

The equality of heights proved above makes this label map unambiguous,
including repeated gradients at different physical times. Let

    delta = min_{0<=a<b<=m} ||g^a-g^b|| > 0.        (5.1)

Choose

    R^2 >= max(1,2A).                              (5.2)

For a physical `i` and a target label `b`, define

    N_{ib}=<z_i-v^{a(i)},v^b-v^{a(i)}>,
    v^b=(g^b,eta^b/R).

When `a(i)!=b`, choose any original representative of `b` (or the reference
label for zero) in (4.2). The possible positive correction is at most
`A(-Q_ji)/R^2<=(-Q_ji)/2`. Thus

    N_{ib} <= Q_ji/2
            <= -(gamma/2)||g_i-g^b||^2
            <= -gamma delta^2/2.                  (5.3)

For equal labels it is identically zero. This retains every PHYSICAL
sample row, even when one vertex label occurs repeatedly; those samples
have different `H_i` and must not be silently collapsed as time indices.

If `g_i=0` and `b!=0`, the exact formula is even more transparent:

    N_{ib}=Q_{ji}-H_i eta^b/R^2<0.

So zero-gradient samples supply strict inequalities against every nonzero
vertex. Their equality against zero itself is a harmless identical-vertex
row, not a missing strictness condition.

The strict margins also show that each distinct nonzero `v^b` is an exposed
vertex of `D_R`: at an occurrence of label `b`, the vector `z_i-v^b`
strictly exposes it among all other generating points. Zero is exposed by
`a_R`, since all `eta^b>0`. Thus, under (5.2), the sparse body already has
exactly `m+1` vertices, although they need not be affinely independent.

## 6. Mechanism 2: an explicit simplex perturbation with exact dynamics

Append `m` new mutually orthogonal coordinates. Let `e_1,...,e_m` be their
standard basis and set `e_0=0`. For a number `epsilon>0`, define

    w^b=(v^b,epsilon e_b),  0<=b<=m,
    D_{R,epsilon}=conv{0,w^1,...,w^m}.

In particular `w^0=0`; a zero-gradient vertex is NOT given a new nonzero
component. Every occurrence of the same nonzero gradient receives exactly
the same component. Define cumulative chronological vectors

    b_i=sum_{t<i} h_t e_{a(t)},
    Z_i=(z_i,-epsilon b_i),
    A_R=(a_R,0).

The INITIAL appended coordinates are zero. Their subsequent values above
are recomputed from all the actual preceding steps, rather than assumed to
stay zero. By construction,

    Z_0=(x_0,-R,0),
    Z_{i+1}=Z_i-h_i w^{a(i)}.                       (6.1)

The normal condition has an explicit perturbation identity. With
`a=a(i)`, for every target label `b`,

    <Z_i-w^a,w^b-w^a>
       = N_{ib}
         -epsilon^2 <b_i+e_a,e_b-e_a>.             (6.2)

There is no term linear in `epsilon`, because old and new coordinate blocks
are orthogonal and the new initial block is zero.

Let `b_{i,a}=<b_i,e_a>` for `a>0`, and take `b_{i,0}=0`. All these numbers
are nonnegative and at most `S`. The coefficient of `epsilon^2` in (6.2)
is exactly

    0                         if a=b;
    b_{i,a}-b_{i,b}+1          if a,b>0 and a!=b;
    b_{i,a}+1                  if a>0 and b=0;
    -b_{i,b}                   if a=0 and b>0.

Hence it is at most `S+1`. Equal-label rows remain exactly zero for every
physical occurrence. At zero-gradient samples the perturbation only makes
the distinct-vertex normal inequality more negative.

Choose, in addition to (5.2),

    0<epsilon^2 <= gamma delta^2/[4(S+1)].          (6.3)

Combining (5.3) and (6.2) gives, for all different labels,

    <Z_i-w^{a(i)},w^b-w^{a(i)}>
         <= -gamma delta^2/4 < 0.                 (6.4)

The identical-label rows are zero. Thus every generator satisfies the normal
condition, and (2.1) proves

    P_{D_{R,epsilon}}(Z_i)=w^{a(i)}

at every physical index, including the terminal. Along with (6.1), this
proves that `Z_i` is the ACTUAL GD run of `F_{D_{R,epsilon}}` under the same
word. This is a quantitative proof of the proposal, not an appeal to
genericity or continuity at a supposedly strict equality.

The vectors `w^1,...,w^m` are linearly independent: projection of a linear
relation to the new coordinate block gives `epsilon` times every coefficient
equal to zero. Therefore this body is a genuine `m`-simplex in its span,
with exactly `m+1` vertices including zero.

The nearby minimum remains exact:

    <A_R,w^b>=-eta^b<0 for b>0,
    ||Z_0-A_R||=||x_0||.                           (6.5)

Thus the whole minimum cone has not been replaced by the origin, and no
large artificial coordinate is paid for in the initial distance.

Finally, every perturbed value has the explicit formula

    F_{D_{R,epsilon}}(Z_i)
      = f_i-C_i/R^2-epsilon^2 beta_i,
    beta_i=<b_i,e_{a(i)}>+||e_{a(i)}||^2/2.         (6.6)

If `a(i)=0`, both `C_i` and `beta_i` are zero and the value is exactly zero.
Otherwise

    beta_i=b_{i,a(i)}+1/2,
    0<beta_i<=S+1/2.

This proves value continuity quantitatively while preserving the original
strict-run horizontal trajectory exactly before compression.

For any desired strict-run terminal value loss `tau>0`, the simultaneous
explicit choices

    R^2 >= max(1,2A,2C_n/tau),
    0<epsilon^2 <= min{
        gamma delta^2/[4(S+1)],
        tau/[2(S+1/2)]
    }                                              (6.7)

make the total loss in (6.6) at most `tau`, while all different-label normal
guards remain strictly negative. Every bound is finite and strictly
positive where a positive perturbation is needed. No uniform lower bound
on `delta`, or uniform upper bound on `A`, is assumed.

## 7. Compression to exactly m dimensions and the own closest radius

The construction so far lives in the original space plus `1+m` coordinates.
Let

    E=span{w^1,...,w^m},  dim E=m,

and let `P_E` be orthogonal projection onto `E`. Since the entire body lies
in `E`, for every `Z` and every `w in D_{R,epsilon}`,

    <Z,w>=<P_E Z,w>,
    ||Z-w||^2=||P_E Z-w||^2+||Z-P_E Z||^2.

Consequently both the value and the selected projection gradient are
preserved:

    F_D(Z)=F_D(P_E Z),
    P_D(Z)=P_D(P_E Z).

Put `q_i=P_E Z_i` and `a=P_E A_R`. Then

    q_{i+1}=q_i-h_i w^{a(i)},
    P_D(q_i)=w^{a(i)},
    F_D(q_i)=F_D(Z_i),
    <a,w^b>=-eta^b<=0.

Thus the compressed points are an actual GD run of the same simplex
function regarded as a function on the `m`-dimensional Euclidean space
`E`; choosing an orthonormal basis identifies it with `R^m`. The point `a`
is a true minimizer, and

    ||q_0-a||=||P_E(Z_0-A_R)||<=||x_0||.            (7.1)

This handles the selected radius. The OWN closest radius is preserved
exactly under the compression as well. Writing `C_E` for the polar cone
inside `E`, the ambient minimum set is

    C_D = C_E + E^perp.

Orthogonal decomposition therefore gives

    dist(Z_0,C_D)=dist(P_E Z_0,C_E).                 (7.2)

If the terminal value is positive, neither starting point is a minimizer:
a zero gradient would leave every following iterate fixed with zero value.
The shared radius in (7.2), denoted `rho`, is then positive, and (7.1) gives

    0<rho<=||x_0||.

For `r=||x_0||>0`, if `tau<f_n`, (6.7) consequently yields

    2 F_D(q_n)/rho^2 >= 2(f_n-tau)/r^2.             (7.3)

The positivity of the lower numerator is explicit; no inequality with a
negative numerator is reversed by changing the denominator. Neither the
selected compressed radius nor the closest radius is asserted to equal the
original `r`. The inequality is sufficient.

The number of distinct sampled positions is at most `p+1`, because a zero
step leaves the position unchanged and each positive step can add at most
one position. Therefore

    m <= p+1,
    number of simplex vertices = m+1 <= p+2.

This count includes the terminal gradient. Repeated gradients can reduce
`m` further, even when their positions differ. It is not legitimate to
remove a distinct terminal gradient merely because it is unqueried by the
last update; it remains part of this value/normal construction.

## 8. Regularization of an arbitrary 1-smooth original run

Return now to an arbitrary convex differentiable 1-smooth `f`, with chosen
minimum zero at zero and initial radius `r>0`. Its original samples are
`x_i,g_i,f_i`. For `0<c<1`, define `f_c=c f` and run the SAME word on it,
starting from the same `x_0`. Denote the new actual positions by `x_i^c`.
Its smoothness bound is `ell=c<1`, and its minimum set is unchanged.

Set

    M=max_{0<=i<=n}||g_i||,
    Pi_i=product_{t<i}(1+h_t),
    B_i=(1-c)M(Pi_i-1).

Subtract the two actual updates and use 1-Lipschitz continuity of `grad f`:

    ||x_{i+1}^c-x_{i+1}||
      <= (1+c h_i)||x_i^c-x_i||+(1-c)h_i||g_i||
      <= (1+h_i)||x_i^c-x_i||+(1-c)h_i M.

Induction gives

    ||x_i^c-x_i||<=B_i.                             (8.1)

Convexity and smoothness at the ORIGINAL terminal point imply

    |f(x_n^c)-f_n|<=||g_n||B_n+B_n^2/2.

Therefore the terminal error after scaling the objective is explicitly

    |f_c(x_n^c)-f_n| <= e_c,
    e_c=(1-c)f_n+c||g_n||B_n+c B_n^2/2 -> 0.        (8.2)

For example, with `K=f_n+M^2(Pi_n-1)+M^2(Pi_n-1)^2/2`, one has
`e_c<=(1-c)K`. For a positive original terminal value, `K>0`, so a finite
choice of `c<1` sufficiently close to one is immediate from this bound.

The exact horizontal reproduction in Sections 4--6 is of the ACTUAL
`f_c` run. There is no assertion that this regularized run is horizontally
identical to the original `f` run.

Given any positive original score and `eta>0`, choose

    0<d<min(f_n,eta r^2/2).

First choose `c<1` so that `e_c<d/2`; the new strict-run terminal value is
positive. Then choose a strict-run loss `0<tau<d/2`, and choose `R,epsilon`
by (6.7) for THAT strict run. Its total value loss relative to the original
is less than `d`, so the resulting simplex run has positive terminal value
and own-closest score

    2 F_D(q_n)/rho^2
      >= 2(f_n-d)/r^2
      > 2f_n/r^2-eta.                              (8.3)

This sequence of choices is important: `c` first, then its finite actual
transcript, then `R`, then a positive `epsilon`, then span compression.
The parameters may depend on the instance, the entire fixed word, and the
tolerance. The number of distinct gradient labels may also depend on `c`,
but it always satisfies the same bound `m<=p+1`.

## 9. Equality of suprema, scale L, and boundary audit

Every simplex function in (1.1) is a legal convex differentiable 1-smooth
function with a minimizer, by Section 2. Thus

    W_n^simplex(h)<=W_n(h).

For every original positive-score instance and every tolerance, (8.3)
produces an admissible simplex instance with no more than `p+2` vertices
and dimension no more than `p+1`. Taking suprema gives the reverse
inequality and proves the candidate identity (1.1).

Original zero-score runs do not require a ratio with zero closest radius.
The restricted class is nonempty and has nonnegative scores. It even has
a positive score for every fixed word: in dimension one take `D=[0,1]`
and start at `q_0=1+S`. Every iterate stays at least one, all projection
gradients equal one, and the terminal value is `1/2`, with closest radius

For arbitrary `L>0`, replace the original function by

    tilde f(x)=[f(x_*+x)-f(x_*)]/L.

The normalized step is `h_i`, exactly corresponding to the original
`h_i/L` step. Multiply the final simplex function by `L`. Its gradient
is `L P_D`, its algorithm again uses the same word, and its normalized
score is still `2F_D(q_n)/rho^2`.

The complete boundary audit is as follows.

## 2. Correlated characters, real metric, and one static body

For each k=0,...,m-1 let tau_k=N-2^k, the character label whose bits
k through m-1 are 1. Let Kmix=N-1-m, and for all nonzero character
labels t in F_2^m define

    b_(tau_k)^2=2^k/(N-1),
    b_t^2=zeta/(N^2 Kmix) for the remaining labels,
    U_s(t)=b_t (-1)^(t dot s).

There are exactly m distinct dominant labels. Every other nonzero
label remains present with strictly positive weight. Let

    M=sum_(t!=0)b_t^2=1+zeta/N^2,
    T=M+R^(-2), w_s=(U_s,1/R).

These are real Euclidean vectors, with the vertical contribution fully
included. Walsh orthogonality follows by pairing labels differing in
one bit:

    sum_s chi_t(s)=0 for nonzero t,
    sum_s chi_t(s)chi_u(s)=N*1_(t=u).

Including the constant row proves the N by N full Walsh matrix is
invertible. Thus the N vectors w_s are linearly independent, as all
coordinate weights and 1/R are positive. Positive radial rescaling
preserves independence. With Gamma(i)=i xor floor(i/2), set

    v_i=sigma_i w_(Gamma(i)), 0<=i<=n,
    D=conv{0,v_0,...,v_n}, C=cone{v_0,...,v_n},
    F_D(z)=max_(g in D) {<z,g>-||g||^2/2}.

This is one full-dimensional simplex in R^N, not an expected Gram or
a changing collection of functions. No universality representation is
used as a proof premise. The cone is independent of the positive
radii and is closed because it is an invertible linear image of the
nonnegative orthant. Its full polar is

    C^polar={(x,y): <x,U_s>+y/R<=0 for EVERY original s}.

Completing the square makes the unique maximizer P_D(z). Its exact
characterization is

    g in D, <z-g,w-g><=0 for EVERY vertex w of D, including 0. (2.1)

The usual two-normal addition directly gives

    <z-z',P_D(z)-P_D(z')> >= ||P_D(z)-P_D(z')||^2.       (2.2)

Comparing the two maximizing affine expressions gives differentiability
with gradient P_D; (2.2) gives 1-Lipschitz continuity. F_D is finite
and convex, and on the open interior of D it equals ||z||^2/2, so its
least Lipschitz gradient constant is exactly 1.

The FULL minimum is

    argmin F_D=C^polar, min F_D=0.                       (2.3)

Indeed the value is zero on the polar. Conversely, if <z,v_i>>0,
then a sufficiently small positive multiple of v_i in D makes the
defining objective strictly positive. In particular z_star=(0,-R)
is a strict polar point, with <z_star,v_i>=-sigma_i. For the required
slice z_0=(x_0,-R), this particular minimum has distance ||x_0||;
the closest minimum may be different. Multiplying F_D by L>0 gives
the same physical GD run and the same W=2R score under step h_i/L.

## 3. Physical ordering and exact overlap identities

Writing the binary bits of i as i_k, Gray bit l is i_l xor i_(l+1),
where i_m=0. The xor sum of Gray bits k through m-1 telescopes, hence

    chi_(tau_k)(Gamma(i))=(-1)^(i_k).                   (3.1)

Thus the dominant physical coordinates run in binary-counter order;
the actual Gray labels have NOT been chronologically permuted. Also,
if l=nu_2(i+1), incrementing i changes bits 0 through l, whose Gray
changes cancel except at l. Therefore

    Gamma(i+1)=Gamma(i)+e_l.

Among all characters, N/2 have bit l set; among the dominant labels,
exactly tau_0,...,tau_l do. The exact flip energies are consequently

    E_l=(2^(l+1)-1)/(N-1)
          +zeta (N/2-l-1)/(N^2 Kmix).                   (3.2)

For the intersection of physical bits 0 and 1, the only dominant label
is tau_0. Of all characters exactly N/4 have both bits set. Thus

    J=1/(N-1)+zeta (N/4-1)/(N^2 Kmix),
    E_1-2J=1/(N-1).                                    (3.3)

For any labels s,u let E(s+u) denote the sum of b_t^2 on characters
with t dot (s+u)=1. Then

    <w_s,w_u>=T-2E(s+u), ||w_s||^2=T.                  (3.4)

For three successive frames with flips l then k, their pairwise
inner products are T-2E_l, T-2E_k, and
T-2E_l-2E_k+4J_lk. This includes the vertical component in every row.

## 1. Statement being audited and the correct quotient

Fix a finite integer `n>=0` and a predetermined word

    S=sum_(i<n) h_i,       p=#{i<n:h_i>0}.

problem, including all finite dimensions, all convex differentiable functions
with gradient Lipschitz constant at most one and an attained minimum, and
every selected minimizer in the denominator.

The audited restricted class consists of

    D=conv{0,w_1,...,w_m} in R^m,
    1<=m<=p+1, with w_1,...,w_m linearly independent,
    F_D(x)=max_(g in D){<x,g>-||g||^2/2}.

The simplex is full-dimensional in its stated Euclidean space. No uniform
angle, aspect ratio, vertex norm, inradius, or bound on the start is imposed.
Its entire minimum set is retained. The audited assertion is

    W_n^simplex(h)=W_n(h).                              (R)

This is equality of suprema for EACH fixed finite word. It does not assert
exact finite-parameter representation of every original run, attainment in
the simplex class, or a single approximation uniform over words or instances.

Let `C_D=argmin F_D`. For an initial point outside `C_D`, the largest
nonnegative payoff over choices of minimizer is attained by a closest one:

    2F_D(T_h x)/dist(x,C_D)^2.

Indeed all selected-minimizer denominators are at least this squared distance,
and a closest point exists. If `x in C_D`, every actual GD iterate stays at
`x` and has zero value. Such starts contribute only zero whenever a legal
nonidentical selected minimizer exists; no quotient `0/0` is formed. Thus
the positive part of the restricted supremum can be taken using the exact
closest-minimum distance without changing the original definition.

For a nonempty compact CONVEX set `D`, completing the square shows that the
unique maximizer defining `F_D(x)` is the Euclidean projection `P_D(x)`.
For `v in D`, the exact characterization is

    P_D(x)=v iff <x-v,w-v><=0 for every w in D.           (2.1)

Necessity follows by differentiating squared distance along segments in `D`.
For sufficiency expand `||x-w||^2` about `v`. When `D` is a finite convex
hull it suffices to test every generator, since the normal expression is
affine in `w`.

Adding the two projection inequalities at `x,x'` gives

    <x-x',P_D(x)-P_D(x')>>=||P_D(x)-P_D(x')||^2.

Therefore `P_D` is 1-Lipschitz. Evaluating each affine maximum at the other's
optimizer gives

    0<=F_D(x')-F_D(x)-<P_D(x),x'-x>
      <=<P_D(x')-P_D(x),x'-x><=||x'-x||^2.

This proves differentiability with gradient `P_D`, and hence global
1-smoothness. Convexity follows from the maximum of affine functions.

When `0 in D`, the exact minimum value is zero and

    C_D={a:<a,g><=0 for every g in D}.                  (2.2)

If `a` obeys these inequalities, every defining term is nonpositive and the
zero generator attains zero. Conversely, if `<a,g>>0`, convexity and `0 in D`
allow `theta*g in D` for arbitrarily small positive `theta`; its objective
term is positive for sufficiently small `theta`. Thus no other point is a
minimizer. `C_D` is the closed convex POLAR CONE, with threshold zero.

Every `x` has a closest point in `C_D`: a distance-minimizing sequence can be
confined to a bounded ball, then compactness and closedness give a minimizer;
strict convexity gives uniqueness. Throughout this audit the exact radius is

    r_D(x)=dist(x,C_D),
